prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A number of recently discovered protein structures incorporate a rather unexpected structural feature: a knot in the polypeptide backbone. These knots are extremely rare, but their occurrence is likely connected to protein function in as yet unexplored fashion. Our analysis of the complete Protein Data Bank reveals several new knots which, along with previously discovered ones, can shed light on such connections. In particular, we identify the most complex knot discovered to date in human ubiquitin hydrolase, and suggest that its entangled topology protects it against unfolding and degradation by the proteasome. Knots in proteins are typically preserved across species and sometimes even across kingdoms. However, we also identify a knot which only appears in some transcarbamylases while being absent in homologous proteins of similar structure. The emergence of the knot is accompanied by a shift in the enzymatic function of the protein. We suggest that the simple insertion of a short DNA fragment into the gene may suffice to turn an unknotted into a knotted structure in this protein.

outputs.L1: Several recently determined protein structures exhibit a rather unexpected structural feature: a knot in the polypeptide backbone. Although such knots are extremely rare, their occurrence is likely linked to protein function in ways that remain unexplored. Our analysis of the complete Protein Data Bank reveals several new knots that, together with those identified previously, may shed light on these connections. In particular, we identify the most complex knot discovered to date in a human ubiquitin hydrolase and suggest that its entangled topology protects the protein from unfolding and degradation by the proteasome. Protein knots are typically conserved across species and, in some cases, even across kingdoms. However, we also identify a knot that occurs only in certain transcarbamylases and is absent from homologous proteins with similar structures. The emergence of this knot is accompanied by a shift in the protein’s enzymatic function. We suggest that the simple insertion of a short DNA fragment into the gene may be sufficient to transform an unknotted structure into a knotted one in this protein.
outputs.L2: Several protein structures identified in recent years contain an unusual feature: their polypeptide backbones form knots. Although such knots are exceedingly uncommon, they may be linked to protein function in ways that remain poorly understood. By examining the entire Protein Data Bank, we found several previously unrecognized knots that, together with known examples, may help clarify these functional relationships. Most notably, human ubiquitin hydrolase contains the most intricate protein knot identified so far; we propose that this entanglement helps prevent the protein from unfolding and being degraded by the proteasome. Protein knots are generally conserved among species and, in some cases, even across biological kingdoms. Nevertheless, we discovered a knot present only in certain transcarbamylases and missing from homologous proteins with comparable structures. Its appearance coincides with a change in the protein’s enzymatic activity. We further propose that inserting a short DNA sequence into the gene could be enough to convert this protein from an unknotted form into a knotted one.
outputs.L3:
Knots in polypeptide backbones are exceptionally rare, and their biological significance remains poorly understood. Nevertheless, their unusual topology suggests that they may influence protein stability, folding, degradation, or function. A comprehensive analysis of structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank identified several previously unrecognized knotted proteins, expanding the known range of protein knot types and highlighting the value of systematic structural surveys.

The most complex protein knot discovered to date occurs in a human ubiquitin hydrolase. This intricate topology may provide mechanical stability, helping the enzyme resist unfolding and subsequent degradation by the proteasome. More broadly, protein knots tend to be evolutionarily conserved: they are often retained across species and, in some cases, even across different biological kingdoms. Such conservation supports the idea that knotted structures can confer important functional or structural advantages.

Transcarbamylases provide a notable exception to this general pattern. Some members of this enzyme family contain knots, whereas closely related and structurally similar homologs do not. In these proteins, the appearance of a knot coincides with a change in enzymatic function, suggesting that knot formation may have contributed to functional diversification. One proposed evolutionary mechanism is the insertion of a short DNA fragment into an ancestral transcarbamylase gene. The resulting additional amino acid segment could have altered the protein’s folding pathway and topology, producing a knotted backbone while simultaneously reshaping the active site and modifying the enzyme’s activity.
outputs.L4:
A systematic survey of structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank was carried out to identify genuine topological knots in protein backbones. Because proteins are open chains rather than closed loops, their termini were extended and joined computationally in ways that minimized the chance of creating an artificial entanglement. The resulting closed curves were then classified by standard knot invariants. This approach revealed several previously unrecognized knots and showed that, within a given protein family, knot type and location are often evolutionarily conserved. Such conservation suggests that these unusual topologies are reproducible consequences of folding and may contribute to protein stability or function rather than being accidental structural features.

The most intricate example was found in a human ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase. Its backbone forms a \(5_2\) knot, substantially more complex than the trefoil knots previously observed in many proteins. The knotted region is deeply embedded in the structure, so complete unfolding would require a large portion of the chain to pass back through a tight loop. This topology could create a mechanical barrier to unfolding by the proteasome. Since proteasomal degradation normally begins by pulling a substrate through a narrow channel, a deeply knotted domain might unfold slowly, resist translocation, or require additional force and processing. The knot may therefore help regulate the lifetime of the hydrolase, although direct experiments are needed to establish its physiological effect.

A second informative case occurs among transcarbamylase enzymes. Certain N-acetylornithine transcarbamylases contain a conserved trefoil knot, whereas closely related ornithine transcarbamylases with a similar overall fold are unknotted. Structural comparison indicates that the knot is associated with changes near the active site and with differences in substrate specificity. The knotted form may have evolved through a relatively short insertion in the ancestral gene: the additional segment could have redirected the backbone through an existing loop during folding, creating the trefoil topology without requiring a major reorganization of the protein’s overall architecture.

Together, these findings show that knots in proteins can be both complex and evolutionarily persistent. Comparisons between knotted proteins and structurally similar unknotted homologs provide clues to how knots arise and what selective advantages they may confer. In some proteins, a knot may enhance mechanical stability or impede degradation; in others, it may reshape an active site and alter enzymatic function. Protein knots thus represent potentially important structural adaptations rather than mere geometric curiosities.
outputs.L5:
### Our Protein, Our Strength

Protein is essential for building muscles, repairing tissues, and supporting overall health. Our bodies rely on this important nutrient every day. These benefits make protein-rich foods—such as eggs, fish, beans, dairy products, and nuts—a valuable part of a balanced diet. By choosing high-quality protein sources, we can support our energy levels, strength, and long-term well-being.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper about newly identified knots in protein structures, their evolutionary conservation, and possible functional significance.
counterfactuals.output: Protein knots are rare structural features in which the polypeptide backbone forms a nontrivial topology, yet their evolutionary origins and biological roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the identification of previously unrecognized knotted motifs in experimentally determined and predicted protein structures using topology-aware computational screening and structural validation. Comparative analyses across homologous families reveal that several knots are conserved despite substantial sequence divergence, indicating that they are maintained by selection rather than arising as incidental consequences of folding. Conserved residues cluster near knot cores, threading regions, and ligand-binding or oligomerization interfaces, suggesting that knot topology may help organize active sites, stabilize mechanically or thermally vulnerable folds, or regulate conformational dynamics. In other families, knots are restricted to particular evolutionary lineages and coincide with insertions, deletions, or domain rearrangements that provide plausible routes for their emergence or loss. These findings expand the known diversity of knotted proteins and support a model in which backbone topology can be both an evolutionarily conserved structural constraint and a source of functional innovation. Experimental characterization of the newly identified proteins will be required to establish the specific contributions of knotting to folding, stability, and activity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a Protein Data Bank analysis that discovered several knotted proteins, including a highly complex knot in human ubiquitin hydrolase and a lineage-specific knot in transcarbamylases.
counterfactuals.output:
A systematic survey of Protein Data Bank structures showed that protein knots are rare but more diverse and deeply embedded than previously recognized. By mathematically closing each protein backbone and classifying its topology, the researchers identified several knotted protein families, including:

- A **five-crossing \(5_2\) knot** in human ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase UCH-L3—the most complex protein knot known at the time. The knot remains intact even after dozens of residues are removed from both termini, indicating that it is deeply embedded rather than an artifact of chain closure.
- A **figure-eight \(4_1\) knot** in ketol-acid reductoisomerases.
- **Trefoil \(3_1\) knots** in several other proteins, including a subset of transcarbamylases.

Comparison of transcarbamylase structures and evolutionary relationships showed that the knot is **lineage-specific**: closely related enzymes can have nearly identical folds while differing in whether one backbone segment passes through a loop. This suggests that the knot arose during evolution through relatively localized structural changes, rather than requiring wholesale redesign of the protein fold.

Overall, the study argued that knots can be conserved architectural features associated with protein stability or function, while also demonstrating that they can appear or disappear over evolutionary time through modest changes in chain connectivity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise scientific paragraph explaining how polypeptide-backbone knots may protect proteins from proteasomal degradation and how short gene insertions could create new knots.
counterfactuals.output: Polypeptide-backbone knots may protect proteins from proteasomal degradation by creating a mechanically resistant topology that impedes ATP-dependent unfolding and passage through the proteasome’s narrow translocation pore. When the proteasome pulls on a terminus, the knot can tighten, increasing the force or time required for substrate processing and thereby slowing or preventing degradation. Short gene insertions could generate new knots by adding a loop or extending a segment that becomes threaded during folding; even a few residues may redirect the folding pathway and convert an otherwise unknotted backbone into a knotted topology. Such effects are strongly dependent on insertion position, sequence, and folding context.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a journal-style abstract on rare topological knots in proteins, highlighting the most complex known example, cross-species conservation, and a knot-associated change in enzyme function.
counterfactuals.output: Although most proteins fold without becoming entangled, a small but expanding set forms reproducible, deeply embedded knots that are integral to the native structure. The most topologically complex natural example characterized to date is the \(6_1\) stevedore knot in the α-haloacid dehalogenase DehI, in which the polypeptide backbone executes six essential crossings. Structural comparisons and sequence analyses indicate that knotted cores are conserved among homologues from evolutionarily distant species, despite substantial divergence in peripheral regions, implying that topology is maintained by selection rather than arising as a folding accident. In α-haloacid dehalogenases, the knotted architecture reorganizes loops surrounding the catalytic pocket and is associated with altered substrate recognition, including a shift from the stereospecific activity typical of unknotted relatives toward dehalogenation of both D- and L-configured substrates. Protein knots therefore represent rare but functionally consequential structural innovations: they constrain folding pathways, stabilize particular active-site geometries, and can support the evolution of new enzymatic properties.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe recent findings on protein knot topology and evolution, with specific discussion of ubiquitin hydrolase, transcarbamylase homologs, and the proposed role of DNA insertion in converting an unknotted protein into a knotted one.
counterfactuals.output:
Protein knots are genuine topological features of the polypeptide backbone: after the open N- and C-termini are closed by a standard computational construction, the chain cannot be reduced to an unknotted circle without crossing itself. Large structural surveys, including predicted-structure databases, indicate that knots remain rare but are strongly concentrated in particular enzyme families. Their family-specific conservation argues that they are usually inherited evolutionary traits rather than accidental folding defects.

### Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases

Ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolases, including UCH-L1 and UCH-L3, contain one of the most complex well-established protein knots—a \(5_2\), or five-crossing, knot. The knot is deep: substantial portions of the chain must be removed from either terminus before the remaining backbone becomes unknotted. Structural and folding studies show that:

- the topology is conserved across the UCH family, suggesting an ancient origin;
- knotting is coupled to a complicated, often slow folding pathway involving intermediates;
- knotting can persist under partly denaturing conditions and may increase resistance to unfolding or proteolytic degradation;
- the knotted core organizes the catalytic domain and loops involved in recognizing ubiquitin, although it is not established that the knot itself was selected directly rather than retained because the surrounding fold and function were selected.

Thus, UCH proteins illustrate both a possible advantage of knots—a compact, mechanically persistent catalytic scaffold—and their evolutionary cost, namely the need for reliable threading during folding.

### Knotted and unknotted transcarbamylase homologs

Transcarbamylases provide an especially informative evolutionary comparison because closely related proteins can have different topology. N-acetylornithine transcarbamylase and related N-succinylornithine transcarbamylases contain a trefoil, \(3_1\), knot, whereas homologous ornithine and aspartate transcarbamylases are generally unknotted. Despite this topological difference, they retain the same broad two-domain architecture and substantial structural and sequence similarity.

Comparisons identify two relevant backbone elements:

1. a loop that forms the “knotting” or encircling loop; and  
2. a later segment, often toward the C-terminal part of the chain, that passes through that loop.

Relatively local changes in loop length and conformation can therefore change the global topology while leaving most of the fold intact. Folding simulations and experiments support threading or slipknot-like routes in which a terminal or near-terminal segment first forms a transient hook and then passes through a preformed loop.

### DNA-insertion hypothesis

The transcarbamylase comparison led to a specific evolutionary proposal: an ancestral unknotted gene acquired a short DNA insertion, producing an extra peptide segment in a surface-loop region. The inserted residues could lengthen or redirect the loop so that, in the folded structure, another part of the chain passed through it. Subsequent substitutions could then stabilize the new geometry, converting an initially unknotted fold into a reproducibly knotted one.

The proposal should not be interpreted as DNA physically tying the protein. Rather, insertion changes the linear amino-acid sequence and hence the preferred three-dimensional folding pathway. It is attractive because it explains how a major topological transition can occur without wholesale redesign of an enzyme. However, insertion alone may not be sufficient: compensatory sequence changes, stabilization of folding intermediates, and selection against misfolding would probably be required. Phylogenetic reconstruction and engineering of loop insertions/deletions support the plausibility of this mechanism, but the exact historical sequence of events remains partly inferential.

Overall, these findings suggest that protein knots can arise through modest genetic changes, become fixed when compatible with folding and function, and then remain highly conserved. UCH hydrolases demonstrate the long-term conservation of a complex knot, whereas transcarbamylase homologs show how closely related proteins can cross the boundary between unknotted and knotted topology.
